Converting the Problem to a Research Framework
(Section 5) explains why you need one. This guide is the procedure for building it.
Most of the research projects in this course move data through the same three stages:
What the sensor recorded (video, audio, logs). Never edited.
not a table — one file per recording
What a model or algorithm extracts from one primary file.
one unit of extraction (a frame, a time window, an event)
Analysis-ready variables derived from the secondary data.

Choose the row meaning for the tertiary table from your research question. In the secondary table, one row might represent one detected frame. If your analysis compares participants’ average knee position, each tertiary row represents one participant: group the frame-level data by
and calculate the participant’s mean knee x- and y-coordinates. If your analysis compares trials instead, each tertiary row represents one trial.
It is a good practice to describe this flow in three passes, each more concrete than the last:

No technical detail yet. Name the
your study tracks (e.g., participant, session, trial, recording, etc.) and draw how data moves between stages. Every arrow must be labelled with the transformation that performs it.

[Entity: participant → session → trial]
              │ record
              ▼
      PRIMARY: one raw file per trial
              │ extract  (model / algorithm)
              ▼
      SECONDARY: one table per raw file
              │ derive + aggregate  (your code)
              ▼
        TERTIARY: one table/dataframe per unit of analysis in analysis-ready format
              │
              ▼
        All the data files of the whole study
              │
              ▼
      statistical analysis
If you cannot name the transformation on an arrow, you have found a gap in your plan.

Pass 3 — Physical: folders, file names, and Python

children.label: Pass 3 — Physical: folders, file names, and Python

children.value: One folder per stage; data only moves downward.

project/
├── data/
│   ├── 01_primary/      # raw files, read-only
│   ├── 02_secondary/    # one table per raw file
│   ├── 03_tertiary/     # one analysis-ready table
│   ├── participants.csv
│   └── sessions.csv
└── notebooks/
Encode the IDs in the name, in a fixed order, separated by underscores:
. No spaces, no “final”, no dates typed by hand. A secondary file keeps the name of the primary file it came from, so the link between them never depends on memory.
